steps.ttsScript: Okay, let's try one together! Here's a little story.

steps.displayText: A fox napped under a tall tree. A bird sang above her.
steps.ttsScript: A fox napped under a tall tree. A bird sang above her.
Who is the story about? That's right, the fox!
Where did it happen? Under a tree!
And what happened? The fox took a nap! You found the character, setting, and event. Amazing job!
Let's try one together! Listen to this.

steps.displayText: The moon is bright, a cozy light.
steps.ttsScript: The moon is bright, a cozy light.
Does it have short lines? Yes, it does!
What kind of writing is it? It is a poem!
Short lines that rhyme tell us it's a poem. You figured it out!
Let's try one together! Here's a new book.
This book is called All About Bugs.
What part shows the title and a picture? The front cover!
Where do we find who made it? The title page inside!
The front cover greets you, and the title page tells who made it. You're a book expert!
Let's try one together! Here's a fact book about bugs.
The book is called All About Beetles.
Who wrote the words? The author!
Who drew the pictures? The illustrator drew them!
The author writes the words and the illustrator draws the pictures. You found them both!
Okay, let's try one together! I'll say a word, and we'll find the beginning and ending sounds.
Here is our word: pig. Say it slowly with me. Pig.
What is the very first sound you hear in pig? That's right, Puh! Pig starts with the letter P.
Now what is the very last sound in it? Guh! Pig ends with the letter G.
So pig starts with Puh and ends with Guh. You found the beginning and ending sounds. Amazing job!
Let's try one together! I'll say a word super slowly, and we'll count every sound.
Here is our word: fish. Let's stretch it out. Ffff-iii-shhh.
Say it slowly with me. Ffff-iii-shhh. We hold up a finger for each sound we hear.
Now count it. Fff is one, iii is two, shhh is three. How many sounds? Three!
So fish has three sounds. You counted every single one. You're a sound detective!
Let's try one together! I'll show you a letter, and we'll say the sound it makes.
Here is our letter: P. Look at it carefully.
What is this letter's name? It is the letter Pee!
And what sound does it make? Puh! Like the start of pop and pig.
So the letter P says Puh. You unlocked another letter sound. Way to go!
Let's try one together! Here is a sight word we read just by looking.
Here is our word: and. You will see it in almost every book.
Can you read it just by looking? It says and!
Do we sound it out? No! It is a sight word, so we just know it, fast as lightning.
So and is a sight word you read right away. One more reading superpower. Nice work!
Let's try one together! Picture this in your mind.

steps.displayText: A girl holds an umbrella. Rain falls from gray clouds.
steps.ttsScript: A girl holds an umbrella. Rain falls from gray clouds.
What is falling in the picture? That's right, rain!
So what kind of weather is it? A rainy day!
The picture told us it is rainy, even with no words. Great reading!
Let's try one together! Here are two books about frogs.

steps.displayText: Book 1: frogs jump. Book 2: frogs swim.
steps.ttsScript: Book one says: frogs jump. Book two says: frogs swim.
Are both books about the same topic? Yes, both are about frogs!
How do these books compare? One tells how it jumps, the other how it swims, so they add facts!
Two books gave us more facts about frogs. You compared like a pro!
Let's try one together! Listen to three sounds.
Here are the sounds: mmm... ooo... p.
How many sounds did you hear? Three sounds!
Now push them together fast. Mmm-ooo-p... Mop!
You blended the sounds into mop. Blending power!
Let's try one together! Here is a word.
The word is bed. Let's stretch it out: b... e... d.
What is the first sound? /b/! It comes at the beginning.
And what is the sound in the middle? /e/!
First /b/, middle /e/, last /d/. You found every sound in bed!
Let us try one together. Here are two words.
Here are the words: up and down.
Are these the same, or opposite? Opposite!
Why are they opposite? Up and down go very different ways.
So up and down are opposites. You connected the words!
Let us try one together. Here is a word.
Here is the word: soggy. Soggy means wet and droopy.
What is soggy in real life? A rainy day puddle!
What else is like it? Cereal left too long in milk gets soggy.
So a wet puddle is soggy. You matched the word to real life!
Let's try one together. Here's a little line from a poem.

steps.displayText: The dry leaves crunched under our boots.
steps.ttsScript: The dry leaves crunched under our boots.
Which word makes a sound you can almost hear? Crunched!
Which sense does it pull in? We hear the crunch!
So crunched is a sensory word we can hear. You found the music!
Let's try one together, word detective. Here's a sentence from a fact book.

steps.displayText: The famished puppy ate every last bite.
steps.ttsScript: The famished puppy ate every last bite of food.
What clue do the other words give? The puppy ate every last bite.
So what does it mean? Famished must mean very hungry!
The clue told us famished means very hungry. Great detective work!
Let's try one together. Here's a short fact.

steps.displayText: The sun is a huge star. It gives us light and heat.
steps.ttsScript: The sun is a huge star. It gives us light and heat.
What is the sun? A huge star!
What does it give us? Light and heat!
You found two facts about the sun. Fact books make you smarter!
Let's try one together. Here's a word.
Here is the word: whale.
Which two letters team up? WH!
What sound does it make? The wh sound at the start!
WH teams up to make one sound. Whale! Phonics power!
Let's try one together. Here's a word.
Here is the word: kite.
Is the vowel long or short? Long I!
How do you know it's long? It says its own name, eye!
Kite has a long I, helped by silent E. You told long from short!
Let's try one together. Here's a longer word.
Here is the word: sunshine.
How do we split it? Sun and shine!
What makes shine a long I sound? The silent E at the end!
Split, read, and blend. Sunshine! You read a two-syllable long vowel word!
Let's try one together. Here's a word with an add-on.
Here is the word: unlock.
What is the prefix at the front? UN!
What does it mean? Not!
So unlock means not locked. You peeled off the prefix!
Let's try one together. Here's a tricky word.
Here is the word: thumb.
Which letter is silent and hides? The B!
Do we say it out loud? No, it stays silent!
So thumb sounds like thum. The B is just for show. You caught the surprise!
Let's try one together. Here's a sight word.
Here is the word: would.
Which letter is silent in this word? The L!
How do we say it? It sounds just like wood!
So would has a silent L and sounds like wood. See it often and you'll know it fast!
Let's try one together. Here's a sentence to read with flow.

steps.displayText: The puppy is lost! Where can he be?
steps.ttsScript: The puppy is lost! Where can he be?
How should we read it? With expression, so it sounds worried and curious!
And the speed? Not too fast, not too slow, just right, like you're talking.
Hear how it sounds like real talking? That's reading with flow. You did it!
Let's try one together. Here's a new word.
Here is the word: preheat.
What is the prefix? PRE!
What does it mean? Before!
So preheat means heat before. Prefix power!
Let's try one together. You see a bold word in your book.
The bold word is habitat. Let's use the glossary.
Where do you look? Flip to the glossary!
Habitat starts with H, so we find it near the start. What letter do we hunt for? H!
The glossary tells us a habitat is an animal's home. You found the meaning!
Let's try one together. Here are two words.
The two words are big and huge.
Do they mean the same or the opposite? The same!
So what do we call them? Synonyms!
Big and huge are synonyms because they mean almost the same. You made the connection!
Let's try one together. Here's a real-life moment.

steps.displayText: Sam went first down the tall slide.
steps.ttsScript: Sam went first down the tall slide. He was not scared at all.
Was Sam scared? No, not at all!
What word fits a kid who is not scared? Brave!
Sam was brave. You matched the word to a real moment. Great work!
Let's try one together. Here's a short fable.

steps.displayText: The slow turtle kept going. He beat the fast, lazy hare.
steps.ttsScript: The slow turtle kept going. He beat the fast, lazy hare.
Who won the race? The slow turtle did!
What's the lesson it teaches? Keep going and don't give up!
So the fable's message is: slow and steady wins. You found the lesson!
Let's try one together. Listen to this little story.

steps.displayText: Rain fell all day. What a wonderful, cozy day, the narrator said.
steps.ttsScript: Rain fell all day. What a wonderful, cozy day, the narrator said.
What does the narrator think about the rain? They think it is cozy and wonderful!
Whose opinion is that? The narrator's, not yours. You might think rain is gloomy!
So we told the two views apart. Great detective work!
Let's try one together. Picture this illustration.

steps.displayText: A sunny meadow with bright flowers and a smiling, dancing girl.
steps.ttsScript: A sunny meadow with bright flowers and a smiling, dancing girl.
Are the colors bright or dark? They are bright and sunny!
So what mood does it set? A happy, cheerful feeling!
Bright colors made a happy mood. You read the picture's feeling!
Let's try one together. Here's a reading plan.
Mia read a long mystery book yesterday. Today she wants something different.
How can Mia mix it up? She can read a poem instead!
Why does it help? A different kind stretches her brain!
A poem mixes up her reading and stretches her brain. You picked a great year of reading!
Let's try one together. Here's a true event.

steps.displayText: The plant wilted because nobody watered it.
steps.ttsScript: The plant wilted because nobody watered it for a week.
What signal word connects them? Because!
What caused it? No water made the plant wilt.
No water caused the plant to wilt. You connected cause and effect!
Let's try one together. Here's a fancy word.
Here is the word: habitat.
Which subject uses it? Science!
What does it mean? An animal's home.
Habitat means an animal's home. You cracked an academic word!
Let's try one together. Here's a question.
You want to find just the word volcano in a science book, fast.
Which text feature lists single words and their pages? The index!
Where do we find it? At the back of the book!
So the index at the back finds the word fast. You used a text feature!
Let's try one together. Here's a picture.
A flower picture has tiny labels pointing to the petals, stem, and roots.
What kind of illustration labels the pieces? A diagram!
What does it show us? The parts of the flower!
So a diagram labels the parts. The picture taught you something new!
Let's try one together. Here's a short fact passage.

steps.displayText: Bees live in hives. They make sweet honey.
steps.ttsScript: Bees live in hives. They make sweet honey.
What is it mostly about? The main idea is bees!
What is one important detail about it? They make honey!
Main idea bees, detail honey. You understood the facts!
Let's try one together. Here's a sentence to read.
We won the big game!
What mood does it show? Excited!
So how should we read it? With a happy, cheery voice!
An excited voice for an excited sentence. That is expressive reading!
Let's try one together. Here is a line of prose.

steps.displayText: The rabbit darted away. His heart was pounding fast.
steps.ttsScript: The rabbit darted away. His heart was pounding fast.
Is this prose or poetry? It is prose! It is written in full sentences.
So how do we read it? Like a story! Speed up your voice to show the rabbit's fear.
We read prose smoothly, like talking. You made it come alive!
Let's try one together, detective. Here is a little story.

steps.displayText: The room was gloomy. No light came in, and Sam felt sad.
steps.ttsScript: The room was gloomy. No light came in, and Sam felt sad.
What is our mystery word? Gloomy! Let's find clues to crack it.
So what does it mean? Dark and sad! The clues said no light came in and Sam felt sad.
Gloomy means dark and sad. You cracked the code, detective!
Let's try one together. Here is a word.
Here is the word: replaying.
Cover the ends. What is the root? Play!
What other words can it build? Player and playful! The root play is the heart of them all.
The root play builds a whole word family. You found the heart of the word!
Let's try one together. Here is a sentence.

steps.displayText: The brave knight was as quiet as a mouse.
steps.ttsScript: The brave knight was as quiet as a mouse.
What type of figurative language is this? A simile! It uses the word as to compare.
So what does it really mean? Very quiet! A mouse is super quiet, so the knight was too.
It is a simile that means very quiet. You found the hidden meaning!
Let's try one together. Here is a sentence from a story.

steps.displayText: Maria was drowning in homework all weekend.
steps.ttsScript: Maria was drowning in homework all weekend.
Is there real water here? No. This is not literal. There is no actual water.
So what does it mean? She had way too much homework, like it was burying her.
Drowning paints a feeling, not real water. You unlocked the figurative meaning!
Let's try one together. Here are two short stories.

steps.displayText: A Greek boy and an African girl each save their village.
steps.ttsScript: A Greek boy and an African girl each save their village.
Are these from the same culture? No. They come from two different cultures.
But what big idea do they share? Courage! Both heroes are brave.
Different cultures, same theme of courage. You compared them like a reader!
Let's try one together. Here's how a reader takes on a long book.

steps.displayText: Sam read one chapter each night. He jotted notes about the brave knight.
steps.ttsScript: Sam read one chapter each night. He jotted notes about the brave knight.
How much did Sam read each day? One chapter. A steady pace makes a long book easy.
What did he take notes about? The knight, a character he wants to remember.
A chapter a day plus notes on characters. Now you can conquer big stories!
Let's try one together. Listen for the details that prove the answer.

steps.displayText: Bats sleep all day in dark caves. They hunt for insects at night.
steps.ttsScript: Bats sleep all day in dark caves. They hunt for insects at night.
When do bats hunt? At night. The text says so right there.
How do you know? Because the text says they hunt at night. That's your evidence.
You backed your answer with text evidence. That's how detectives read nonfiction!
Let's try one together. Find what the whole passage is mostly about.

steps.displayText: Bees collect nectar. They make honey. They help flowers grow. Bees are busy helpers.
steps.ttsScript: Bees collect nectar. They make honey. They help flowers grow. Bees are busy helpers.
What is the main idea? Bees are helpers. That ties every sentence together.
Is making honey the main idea? No, it is just one detail under the big idea.
The main idea is the umbrella; honey is rain underneath. You found the heart of the text!
Let's try one together. Here's a sentence with an academic word.
The scientist made a prediction before the test began.
steps.displayText: The scientist made a prediction before the test began.

steps.ttsScript: What is the academic word? Prediction!
What does it mean? A guess about what will happen.
So prediction means a guess about what will happen. You used the context to unlock it!
Let's try one together. Listen to this short passage.
First, mix the flour. Next, add eggs. Finally, bake the cake.
steps.displayText: First, mix the flour. Next, add eggs. Finally, bake the cake.

steps.ttsScript: What clue words do you hear? First, next, finally!
What text structure is it? Sequence!
So the clue words tell us it is sequence. You spotted the structure!
Let's try one together. Listen to this passage.
In 1849, thousands of miners traveled west to find gold.
steps.displayText: In 1849, thousands of miners traveled west to find gold.

steps.ttsScript: Was the writer there? No!
So what kind of account is it? Secondhand!
It gives facts and dates, not feelings, so it is secondhand. You figured it out!
Let's try one together. Here's a long word.
Here is the word: fantastic.
How do we chunk it? Fan, tas, tic!
Now blend the chunks together. Fantastic!
You chunked it, read it, and blended it into fantastic. You decoded the whole word!
Let's try one together. Here's a sentence to read aloud.
Here is the sentence: Suddenly, the rocket blasted off!
Should we read it fast or slow? This is action, so read it fast!
How should it sound? Excited! Let your voice show the action.
So we speed up and sound excited. That's smooth reading!
Let's try one together. Here's a sentence with a clue.

steps.displayText: The cave was murky, or dark and dim.
steps.ttsScript: Here is the sentence: The cave was murky, or dark and dim.
What signal word points to a clue? The word or!
So what does murky mean? Dark and dim! The clue told us.
Murky means dark and dim. The sentence gave you the clue!
Let's try one together. Here's a reading problem.

steps.displayText: You want a stronger word than happy.
steps.ttsScript: Here is the problem: You want a stronger word than happy.
Which tool helps? A thesaurus, because you need a similar word!
What does it give you? Synonyms, like joyful or thrilled!
So a thesaurus swaps happy for joyful. Right tool, right job!
Let's try one together. Here's an idiom.
Here is the idiom: piece of cake.
Is it about real cake? No! Idioms have a hidden meaning.
So what does it mean? Very easy! Like, the test was easy.
Piece of cake means very easy. You cracked the hidden meaning!
Let's try one together. Here's a word with an ending.
Here is the word: played.
What ending do you see? E-D, the -ed ending!
When did it happen? It already happened! The -ed tells us it is done.
So played means it already happened. You read the ending!
Let's try one together. Here's a tricky word.
Here is the word: of.
How is it spelled? O-F! But it does not sound that way.
Can we sound it out? No! We just memorize it by sight.
So of breaks the rules. We know it by sight. Great job!
Let's try one together. Here's a word.
Here is the word: ball.
Can you point to a ball? Yes! You can hold it and point to it.
So what job does it do? It names a thing, so it is a noun!
So ball is a noun. It names a thing. You spotted the job!
Let's try one together. Here's a sentence.
We want to show the hat belongs to the cat. The cat hat.
What mark shows owning? An apostrophe and an S!
Where does it go? Right after the word cat.
So we write cat's hat. The apostrophe and S show owning. Great work!
Let's try one together. Here's a sentence.
Sam won the race. Sam was very happy.
Could a stronger word paint a clearer picture than happy? Yes!
What word is stronger than happy? Thrilled!
So Sam was thrilled paints a stronger picture. You picked the perfect word!
Let's try one together. Here's a verb.
Here is the verb: run.
Do we just add E-D to make runned? No! Run is a tricky verb that changes.
What is the past tense of it? Ran!
So run becomes ran, not runned. You caught that tricky verb!
Let's try one together. Here is a weak word to fix.
Here is the word: said. The duck said. That word is weak.
Which word is weak and plain? Said! It does not paint a picture.
What stronger word could we use instead? Quacked! Now you can hear the duck.
So the duck quacked beats the duck said. Strong words paint pictures. Great work!
Let's try one together. Here is a sentence that needs a comma.

steps.displayText: She ran fast but she fell.
steps.ttsScript: Here is the sentence: She ran fast but she fell.
Which word joins the two complete sentences? But! That is the conjunction.
Where does the comma go? Before it! The comma comes right before the conjunction.
So we write: She ran fast, comma, but she fell. Comma before the conjunction. You nailed it!
The middle is the biggest part of the story. It is everything that happens after the beginning, before the very end.
Say a puppy got lost at the start. In the middle, the puppy looks and looks for home. The middle holds the action! Always tell the middle, not just the beginning and end.
Two books can share the same topic but still teach you new facts. That is what makes comparing fun.
Both books are about frogs, so the topic is the same. But one book says frogs hop, and the other says frogs eat bugs. Same topic, different new facts. Now you have learned two things!
Watch how one word changes everything. Here is a plain sentence: She walked to the door.
Now I will swap in a feeling word. She stomped to the door. Stomped makes me feel that she is angry! The very same girl, but one word tells me how she feels inside.
Let me show you a detective trick. Here is the sentence: Park your bike here. The word park could mean a green park with grass, or it could mean to stop and leave something.
So I try one meaning and ask, does it make sense? Stop and leave your bike here. Yes! That makes sense. The green-grass park does not fit. Trying the meaning shows me which one is right.
Let's try one together, detective. Here's a sentence.

steps.displayText: Mom had to reread the page because she lost her place.
steps.ttsScript: Mom had to reread the page because she lost her place.
What word part do you see at the front? Re! And re means again.
So what does reread mean? Read again!
The part re plus the clue lost her place both point to again. You cracked the case!
Let's try one together. Here's a phrase.

steps.displayText: It was raining cats and dogs all afternoon.
steps.ttsScript: It was raining cats and dogs all afternoon.
Are cats and dogs really falling from the sky? No! So this is nonliteral.
What does it really mean? It is raining very hard!
The words sound silly literally, so the meaning is nonliteral. You pictured it!
Let's try one together. Here's a brand-new word.
Here is the word: curious. It means wanting to learn more.

steps.displayText: Say it where? In a sentence!
steps.ttsScript: Where should you try it? Say it in a real sentence!

steps.displayText: Try it now: I am curious!
steps.ttsScript: Try it now. I am curious about space! Using it makes it stick.
You used a new word in real talk. Use it again tomorrow and it's yours for life!
Let's try one together. Here's a big word.
Here is the word: investigate. It means to look into something closely.
Is investigate a casual word or an academic word? Academic!

steps.displayText: Use it where? In a report!
steps.ttsScript: So where does it fit best? In a school report, not a chat with friends!
You matched a big word to the right setting. That's how smart writers sound clear!
Let's try one together. Here's a word.
Here is the word: phone.
Which combo do you see? PH!
What sound does it make? F!
So PH says F. Phone! You spotted the combo!
Every smart question has an answer hiding right in the words. Read closely to find it.
Let's try one together. Here's a short story.

steps.displayText: Rosa shared her umbrella with a soaked stranger. She walked home in the rain.
steps.ttsScript: Rosa shared her umbrella with a soaked stranger. She walked home in the rain.

steps.displayText: What did she do? Shared umbrella.
steps.ttsScript: What did Rosa do? She shared her umbrella!
What does that show? She is kind!
The action showed kindness, even without the word kind. You read deep!
